images.caption: Figure 1:Architect-Ant transforms an empty structured floor plan into a furnished 3D scene.
Figure 2:AntPlan floor plans with structural, room, and furniture annotations.

Figure 3:Data preparation and training. Detector-assisted annotations form room-level examples for supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO with final-layout rewards. A separate LoRA adapter is trained for each room category.

Figure 4:Inference and 3D scene construction. Room geometry, a structure-only image, and a retrieved furniture request condition the room adapter to generate a reasoning trace followed by an editable DSL layout. Layouts are scored and selected before 3D assets are retrieved and rendered.

Figure 5:3D visualizations on shared room shells for bathrooms, kitchens, living rooms, and bedrooms. Learned 3D-FRONT baselines are shown only for supported room categories. The scenes provide qualitative comparisons; quantitative evaluation is performed on the layout geometry.
Figure 6:An annotated AntPlan example. Left: the original architectural drawing. Center: structural and object bounding boxes with semantic labels. Right: annotated room regions and room categories.

images.caption: Figure 7:Three illustrative pairs from the whole-house preference study, preserving the evaluated A/B assignments. Method labels and outcomes are added here for the reader; the judge saw anonymous images. Claude Sonnet 5 favored Architect-Ant in (a) for its visible kitchen and clearer circulation, and in (b) for its cooking/dining setup and complete bathroom. It favored SceneSmith in (c) for clearer circulation and separation of living and sleeping areas. These reasons reflect the judge’s interpretation of the images. House numbers are export indices, and paired images show different floor plans.
